summary_html: Immediate state action to **protect a child in imminent danger**. Federal law (ASFA/IV-E) ties funding to court findings on **reasonable efforts**, and constitutional limits (due process, 4th/14th Amendments) constrain warrantless removals.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — reasonable-efforts findings; permanency timelines  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal oversight of removal decision quality  
- **Constitutional constraints** — enforced via §1983 actions; due process & search/seizure jurisprudence (not listed in file but governs practice)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Rogers v. County of San Joaquin
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: A social worker who removed children without a warrant was denied qualified immunity because no exigency existed; the agency's own decision to treat the report as a non-emergency ten-day response, and its ability to obtain a warrant within hours, defeated any claim of imminent danger.
key_cases.relevance: Holds that the availability of a warrant within hours defeats a claim of protective-custody exigency.
key_cases.quote: Here, the concerned officials classified the case as a ten-day response, indicating that they did not think that any exigency existed.

key_cases.case_name: State, Department of Health & Social Services, Office of Children's Services v. Michelle P.
key_cases.holding: CINA jurisdiction derives from the child's status as a child in need of aid and is distinct from a custody or supervision grant, so dismissal of the petition was reversed; separately, the removal order was vacated because it lacked sufficient evidentiary support and did not satisfy ICWA.
key_cases.relevance: Vacates a removal order for evidentiary insufficiency, the direct check on protective-custody decisions.
key_cases.quote: This was error because the removal order was not supported by sufficient evidence and did not comply with the requirements of the Indian Child Welfare Act (ICWA).

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: A State may not remove children from a parent's custody without a hearing on that parent's fitness; denying such a hearing to unwed fathers while granting it to all other parents violates due process and equal protection.
key_cases.relevance: Fixes the constitutional rule that protective custody must be followed by a prompt adversarial hearing on parental fitness, which Alaska implements as the AS 47.10.142(d) temporary-custody hearing.
key_cases.quote: We have concluded that all Illinois parents are constitutionally entitled to a hearing on their fitness before their children are removed from their custody.

key_cases.case_name: Wallis ex rel. Wallis v. Spencer
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: Summary judgment for the city was reversed: a jury could find the officers lacked reasonable cause to seize the children without a court order, and, absent a risk that physical evidence would dissipate or an urgent medical problem requiring immediate attention, the state must notify parents and obtain judicial approval before subjecting a seized child to an investigatory physical examination.
key_cases.relevance: Holds that a warrantless protective seizure requires specific, articulable evidence of imminent danger and that its scope must be strictly circumscribed by the exigency that justified it.
key_cases.quote: the state is required to notify parents and to obtain judicial approval before children are subjected to investigatory physical examinations

key_cases.case_name: State, Department of Family & Community Services, Office of Children's Services v. Karlie T.
key_cases.holding: The superior court's dismissal of an emergency CINA petition was reversed in part: the inquiry at that stage is only whether probable cause exists to believe the child is in need of aid, and the domestic-violence evidence sufficed under AS 47.10.011(6) and (8)(B)(i), though (8)(B)(ii) requires that the child actually have been exposed to domestic violence.
key_cases.relevance: Is Alaska's controlling recent decision on the AS 47.10.142 emergency-custody pathway and the showing OCS must make to keep a newborn in temporary custody.
key_cases.quote: we reiterate that the superior court was tasked with making a probable cause determination, not a finding whether the child actually was in need of aid

mandatory_reporters: Practitioners of the healing arts — Alaska Stat. § 47.17.020(a)(1)

School teachers and school administrative staff of public and private schools, including athletic coaches — Alaska Stat. § 47.17.020(a)(2); an unpaid volunteer athletic coach is not required to report unless the coach volunteers more than four hours a week for four consecutive weeks or more than 20 hours a week in a one-month period, has received the training required under Alaska Stat. § 47.17.022, and has signed a form acknowledging the duty to report — Alaska Stat. § 47.17.020(j)
Peace officers and officers of the Department of Corrections — Alaska Stat. § 47.17.020(a)(3)
Administrative officers of institutions — Alaska Stat. § 47.17.020(a)(4)
Paid employees of domestic violence and sexual assault programs and of crisis intervention and prevention programs — Alaska Stat. § 47.17.020(a)(6)
Paid employees of an organization that provides counseling or treatment to people seeking to control their use of drugs or alcohol — Alaska Stat. § 47.17.020(a)(7)
Members of a child fatality review team or of the multidisciplinary child protection team — Alaska Stat. § 47.17.020(a)(8)
Volunteers who interact with children in a public or private school for more than four hours a week — Alaska Stat. § 47.17.020(a)(9)
Juvenile probation officers and juvenile probation office staff, and staff of juvenile detention and juvenile treatment facilities — Alaska Stat. § 47.17.020(a)(10)
reporting_details: Alaska is not a universal-reporting state: only the occupational categories listed in Alaska Stat. § 47.17.020(a) are required to report, and they must report immediately — defined as no later than 24 hours (Alaska Stat. § 47.17.290(7)) — to the nearest office of the Department of Family and Community Services, the department in which the Office of Children's Services sits (Alaska Stat. § 47.17.290(6)); if the harm appears to result from a suspected sex offense they must also report immediately to the nearest law enforcement agency. A reporter who cannot reasonably contact the nearest office of the department when immediate action is necessary for the child's well-being must instead report to a peace officer (Alaska Stat. § 47.17.020(c)). Any other person may report but is not required to (Alaska Stat. § 47.17.020(b)). OCS takes reports at 1-800-478-4444 or 907-269-6510, 24 hours a day, every day, and takes a written report by email at ReportChildAbuse@alaska.gov or by fax at 907-269-3939.

timeline_requirements.requirement_name: Notice to parents of emergency custody
timeline_requirements.deadline: Immediately, and in no event more than 24 hours
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Department takes emergency custody of the child
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Statute sets no penalty; the only excuse it allows is lack of communication facilities (AS 47.10.142(c))

timeline_requirements.requirement_name: Child in need of aid petition filed after emergency custody
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: If the child is released instead, the department must file a report with the court within 24 hours of the release (AS 47.10.142(c))
